review_text: I don't really understand all the hype around Nelson; he comes across as a condescending teacher. For 335, the first midterm felt like a chore, requiring you to memorize a bunch of random information. The only effective way to prepare was by studying previous midterms. For fall 2024, our midterms were nearly identical to those from the previous spring, but they’re always subject to change—spring 2024's midterm, for example, wasn’t like fall 2023's. Our semester got lucky with similar midterms, but overall, you don’t learn much in this class. I was in the 8 AM section, and while I didn’t mind the early timing, Nelson's lectures were quite boring. He often makes jokes and gets off-topic, which isn’t what I want to deal with at 8 AM. It feels like he doesn’t fully understand the material he's teaching. When asked for specifics, he often can’t provide clear answers. If something in his code doesn’t work, he doesn’t seem to know why. I already knew the basics of HTML and CSS but wanted to learn more about JavaScript and MongoDB. Unfortunately, I was disappointed—Nelson simply gave us the code for those topics without explaining how the systems work. The final exam was super easy and almost identical to Project 5. You could literally reword that project and still get full points on the final. The TAs are often PhD or master’s students, and they’re difficult to work with. They don’t provide helpful answers most of the time. This class is definitely worth taking if you’re in it for the grade, but it has its downsides. For example, the midterms aren’t given during class; instead, they’re held at 6:30 PM in a different lecture hall. While I understand Nelson’s intent to prevent one section from sharing answers with another, this setup is inconvenient. I would much prefer taking the midterms during class. Overall, I think 335 needs to be restructured. It feels outdated and poorly designed. We had to learn things from JavaScript ES5, which is deprecated—why bother teaching it? I wish they’d reduce the focus on CSS and introduce more relevant topics, like React, into the projects. A more modern framework would make this course much more worthwhile.

review_text: This class was unreal. Thankfully, there's an online CMSC417 review document you can find on Reddit that contains notes for all of the topics covered in the entire class. This was my only saving grace. The exams were incredibly difficult. He gave practice exams, which was good, but they had no answer key. Without an answer key, it's really hard to know if you're on the right track or not. However, it is very difficult to fully complete the projects in time. The projects are also graded super harshly, as they expect that your implementation is 100% complete. Each individual test case is worth so many points that if you missed just a couple of edge cases, your project grade may only be around 75% at most. For most of the projects, the class average was in the 60s. Also, it's worth mentioning that doing these projects may come at the expense of your performance in other classes. review_text: As others have said, Archana is a very very kind person (regardless of what you think about her teaching). She tries to get to know every student in class, especially those who go to lecture and remain active in office hours. She has lectures which are pretty well organized. She first explains some of the theoretical concepts, and then does some textbook problems on the board or on chalk. She has this raw and updated lecture note system which you'll learn more about if you take her course that is pretty helpful for some (for me, I never had the time to look at the notes before most lectures in the first place and didn't have an iPad so it wasn't particularly remarkable). If you don't use an IPad to take notes, definitely go to her office prior to class to get print-outs of the notes so you can have some of the notes already there that way you won't have to write problems or long theorems that she won't spend more than 2-3 minutes on by hand. Regarding her teaching, I will say there are times where it feels like she doesn't know the topic in depth (especially in stats). For example, she struggled to explain Bessel's correction for sample standard deviation the first time it was taught in class. This doesn't interfere to teach what she thinks is necessary for the course and exams, but it gives off a murky vibe if you're interested in going a bit more beyond surface depth of what's taught in the course and if that interest comes out in the form of asking more complicated questions in class, especially for some of the things in the hypothesis-test section of the course. There are typically quizzes and worksheets in the class that are done on ELMS/Canvas every lecture or so with some being graded and others being for practice. Archana tends to be lenient about this but it can be a pain in the ass to do sometimes, especially because (this is a me thing specifically), I would get lazy and just use GPT or some other thing to do them instead of doing them by hand. There are also projects in the course, but I also used GPT on those. While they give real world applications to what is being taught in the class, they're really just extra work that doesn't correlate with the exams and some of the material we need to know so a lot of people would do the least amount of work possible for them. Now, it is also worth mentioning, I do fundamentally dislike the curriculum for the course. It is pretty much ALL performing hypothesis tests, which are rarely performed anymore by hand (yay for computers). So, you end up getting an extremely in-depth introduction to how to use various hypothesis tests to understand and analyze different data trends, but a lot of this information is useless in modern day statistics simply because machines can do a lot of it for us. While she strived to give a big picture analysis of how to use the techniques (something that would last a lot longer than the individual mathematical techniques we learned to perform each of the tests in the class), I will say that the impression I got was that the class was simply focussed on performing many of these tests by hand and not taking a set of data and deciding what to do with it in order to determine the trends. I would have preferred if we maybe cut the time we spent on discussing how to compute various sources of error, and strict computations of the different hypothesis tests (during the course, you will study one-sample and two-sample z-tests for means and proportion, t-tests for means, confidence intervals, power and error in various tests, anova tests, chi-squared error of tests, error of linear regression with normal residuals, and using the central limit theorem to discuss normal random variables or random variables that converge to the normal distribution), and instead discussed how to decide which statistical tests to use for a given set of data, and how to run such experiments: for example, "how would you go about setting a statistical procedure to get data for determining whether this new feature increases user engagement on a site?". Learning a bit more about sampling (just an introduction), deciding how to filter data, and then picking the hypothesis test and describing the procedure, would have probably been more helpful for your average person who might go into a stats/data-science field in their life at this point of time with technology. This all being said, this is a very very common thing among all STAT401 courses and I suspect this is more of a departmental curriculum thing than it is Archana's fault. Thus, I will not take this out on her rating. BUT, if you're a student, be prepared that the class is heavily computation-focussed, and you will have to learn how to apply some of the techniques to broad data on your own, or in other CMSC/STAT classless such as STAT440, CMSC320, CMSC471, etc The last thing that is worth mentioning about Archana is that, especially in my semester, she sometimes did call people out in class. If you weren't paying attention, she would probably ask "why weren't you paying attention" or something in a kind way (not aggressive at all and you can definitely say "I don't know"). During exams, she would sometimes say how specific individuals did -- let's suppose there is a student named "Arnav" in the class, she might say something like "Arnav, you didn't get that topic on the exam, why did you not get it? Did you not prepare and do the practice problems? Were you not slow enough on the exam?"... things like that can sometimes be huge turn-offs for those who really respect their privacy on exams. She is NEVER doing this out of malice however, and you will notice that even if she does it, she's doing it in a respectful and encouraging way trying to uplift and encourage students to put more time and effort in the course. Just something worth noting for shy students. Overall, Archana is a very kind person, and you should definitely get to know her regardless of your interest, performance, and participation in the class by going to her office hours and simply showing up at every lecture and striving to sit in the front and remain somewhat engaged. Her accent is absolutely fine and easy to understand, and you're going to learn a lot in the course.

There's relational algebra and functional dependencies, E/R modeling, database implementation, then NoSQL stuff, and finally transactions. That's a vast array of topics, and they're done in a strange order, too. This class needs to be whittled down a lot. Focus much more on the SQL and NoSQL stuff. review_text: As I am writing this, Justin's average rating on Planet Terp is a 4.69, which is even higher than Christopher Kauffman's average rating (4.63). I had Kauffman for CMSC216 in Spring 2025, and he was one of my favorite professors of all time. Needless to say, given all the hype around Justin, I had high hopes going into his Summer 2025 CMSC351 class. Now that everything's over, I can say in short that I am disappointed with my experience. To be clear, Algorithms as a Computer Science class is commonly agreed to be a terrible class pretty much everywhere (based on talking to many people from many different universities). A large part of this is due to the fact that those with minimal experience in algorithmic programming find the class extremely difficult, while at the same time those with a lot of experience in algorithmic programming (i.e. competitive programmers, like myself) often dislike how it is taught very mathematically rigorously yet with little intuition or application at all (in other words, this class will not get you through a coding interview). Yes, Algorithms, the Computer Science class, is more of a math class than anything else. Yes, Computer Science is not just programming, and Theoretical Computer Science consists almost entirely of pure math. All of this I knew going in. None of this prepared me for when I lost over half the points on a problem from Homework 1 asking me to prove the Big Omega of a certain function. I approached it as almost everyone intuitively would; like almost everyone had been taught to solve an inequality since middle and high school. Set up the inequality. Turn it into an equality, and solve the equality. Determine which side of the solution to the equality contains the solutions to the inequality, and turn the solution to the equality back into an inequality. Apparently, this wasn't rigorous enough for this class. Perhaps this is just how this kind of stuff works. But we were never told that solving it this way would lose us points, and the "correct" way shown in lecture seemed unnecessary and unintuitive. Instead, Justin complained that many submitted solutions to such Big-Omega or Big-O proof problems looked the way AI would solve them, and that such proofs "were generally terrible", citing several reasons why. Okay, fine. If you take Justin, make sure you explain the hell out of any answer you give to a problem. One problem on Exam 1 asked me to find a lower bound for something and to show my work. I later received minimal points for my answer, despite the fact that the work I had shown lined up almost exactly with a potential full-score answer as described in the rubric. Upon submitting a regrade request, I was told the grader had no idea what I did here at all, since I had no explanation at all. But the question never asked me to explain! Too bad. There was an Exam 1 MCQ problem which asked whether a certain algorithm was O(N^2) in the best case. The algorithm in question was O(N) in the best case and O(N^2) in the worst case. As such, most people in the class answered incorrectly, as technically an algorithm which is O(N) is also O(N^2). A big stink was made on Piazza about this being a trick question hidden in a sea of 50 multiple-choice questions, designed to make students lose points even if they understood the concepts it was supposed to be testing. One student asked, to avoid confusion, why didn't Justin instead ask if the algorithm was O(N^100) in the best case? Another student literally included a screenshot of the Merriam-Webster entry for "trick question" in their post. In the end, Justin's response was that technically the algorithm was indeed O(N^2) in the best case, and that he didn't expect his students to autopilot any questions in his class. On top of this, there was a question on the Exam 2 MCQ which, depending on your interpretation of the question (the wording was not specific enough), could have had two different answers. However, if you picked the wrong one, you had no recourse, not even through Piazza. By this point, people had long since stopped posting on Piazza about questions like this. They knew nothing would result from their efforts. On Exam 3, there was a free-response question which essentially asked us to find the shortest path between two points in "a simple, connected graph" (I'm simplifying greatly). Many test takers realized quickly the looseness of this wording and realized that, to cover all graphs which could potentially be described as "a simple connected graph", one needed to run Floyd's Algorithm, as a simple BFS would not cover the case of a weighted graph, and Dijkstra's would not cover the case of negative-weight edges. Once Exam 3 was graded, everyone who wrote such a solution to that problem lost points (there was a special "tier" in the Gradescope "rubric" for Floyd/Dijkstra solutions). I asked in my regrade request what the issue with my answer was. The response was that I needed to specify what my input to Floyd's Algorithm was or what graph I was going to run it on. I responded that in my answer I had specified running Floyd's algorithm on precisely the graph described in the problem statement. The response? "It does not define distances". Confused and a little frustrated, I wandered over to take a look at the official Exam 3 solutions. The official solution to that problem? Run a BFS. Justin is not the worst professor I've ever had (currently, that (dis)honor goes to Manoussos Grillakis). Justin is not the devil. Justin is not someone who you need to avoid at all costs. But as a student in his Summer 2025 CMSC351 class, I felt like the environment I was in was just a little bit more hostile than I was used to. Every time I made a Piazza post, I was just a little bit nervous that I'd get flamed by Justin in his response. I felt a severe lack of benefit of the doubt, almost to the point of actively trying to take away points from correct or mostly correct answers. Look. Everyone's different, and everyone is looking for different things in the professors they get. Lord knows I have some unpopular opinions regarding some UMD professors (both positively and negatively). You might enjoy Justin when you take him, or he might even have just been going through something this summer. All I'm saying is, if you do decide to take him (and, to be honest, given that the alternative is Kruskal, you might decide to take him anyway): don't say I didn't warn you.

review_text: Dr. Goytia is a genuinely kind and supportive professor who truly wants her students to succeed. She provides all assignments and lecture slides at the beginning of the semester, which is helpful for planning your studies. However, her lectures can feel a bit unorganized, and the slides are difficult to follow on their own without her explanations. Fortunately, Dr. Goytia records all her lectures, allowing you to replay them while reviewing her slides, which is a great resource. She also offers a practice exam before each test and gives students the opportunity to earn three extra credit points for test corrections after every midterm. While "extra credit" might sound exciting, keep in mind that these points only add up to 9 out of 1,000 total class points, so their impact is minimal. On the plus side, you're allowed to bring a one-sided cheat sheet for each exam, including the final, which can be incredibly helpful. Study every diagram on her lecture slides thoroughly, as two of them will appear on each midterm, requiring you to label them. You can even print these diagrams and include them on your cheat sheet. Pay close attention to the wording of her True or False questions—they can be tricky. For the lab, which makes up 42% of your grade, memorize every diagram on the lab slides. Using Anki for this is highly effective.

review_text: Whether or not I remember anything about the complement system or taxonomy, the collective crashout of BSCI223 in Spring 2025 will not be forgotten. Reading the reviews below, you'd think this class was a battlefield—Professor Buchner committing some kind of academic treason and students having to sacrifice their souls to pass. But honestly? It's not 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 bad. I promise. Yes, the flipped lecture style sucks. It's hard to stay motivated to watch the videos or show up to class just to answer clicker questions that are usually very unhelpful in actually understanding the material. Like many others, I signed up for an in-person class—not two mandatory discussions a week + learning the actual content on my own by myself. And exams were tough, but not necessarily because of the material. The issue was the lack of guidance provided to help us prepare. There were no practice exams, no review guides, and barely any clarity on what to focus on (and again, the lectures in class often did not correlate to the videos AT ALL) until the TA's stepped in with some reviews. Professor Buchner's exam format leans heavily on drawing and description questions, which personally caught me off guard. Paired with disorganized and dull lectures, this wasn't exactly a fun class. All that said, getting an A is definitely doable if you put in a modicum of effort. If you've taken genetics, exam 2 should be a breeze, and if you go in having actually studied the material, exam 1 and the final should go well enough that you're in good territory (note: I didn't put enough effort studying for exam 1 and studied the wrong things, which again, was both my fault as well as the course's for NOT TELLING US WHAT TO STUDY but if you go in expecting it to be hard, I guarantee you that you'll do better). Additionally, the lab portion of the class offers a MASSIVE grade buffer. There's a lot of busy work (designing the cow transformation experiment was fun, but making us do like 3 discussion posts/essays/lit reviews each was too much), and bad groupmates will make you curse your life, but the TA's grade really generously, the labs are short and often end early, and they're easy to understand and even a little fun to do. Point is: this class isn't the free ride you think it will be, but it's not that bad. Maybe 3-6 hours of studying per exam plus keeping on track with assignments, and you'll be okay.

review_text: I think people are too harsh on Herman; his average here is a 3.14, which isn't terrible, but the way I've heard older CS students speak about him is as if he is the teacher of doom and despair. (Note that I called him teacher DO NOT call him professor this will be the first thing he says on the first day and he may even spend 10 minutes giving a whole presentation on it later in the sem!) The project descriptions are quite lengthy, but personally I would prefer this to vague descriptions where you have to figure it out yourself. There will be pretty much no questions left unanswered. Some projects are quite difficult, but honestly some of the ones I struggled with the most were also the ones I left until the last day or two, so I would recommend starting around three to four days before the due date. Also, make sure you read through the whole project description before starting, I know it's annoying but it's better than if you start to code and then realize you're violating project requirements, because sometimes you are prohibited from doing things that may be intuitive. Overall though, some projects were hard, some were easy, and also bombing one or two projects is really not detrimental to your grade. He also has some nice extra credit for a lot of them if you do it early and only submit once which is super nice. As for exams, I genuinely think his exams were extremely fair. Herman gives super long practice exams that I usually found to be harder than the actual exam, if not about the same. To study I typically reviewed his slideshows, which he posts, and then did those practice exams and I did pretty well on all the exams. Even questions I got wrong on exams, I felt like they were fair questions to have been asked and things I should have known. One interesting policy to take note of, though, is the grading of multiple choice questions. These were usually the harder part of the exams. They are multi-select and you get 1 point off for selecting an incorrect answer and 2 points off for not selecting a correct answer. This is super important because if you are truly unsure, you should just select an answer because you lose less points if that's wrong than if you don't pick it and it's correct. The lectures themselves can be pretty boring, but I do think they are super helpful. In hindsight, my worst project grade was definitely as a result of me zoning out in class when going over that topic. If you listen in class, you will be pretty set because he does explain concepts well and often uses people in the front row as examples, which helps get the point across. Also, he does like to make jokes sometimes during lectures and personally I really enjoy his humor. The lectures are not necessarily mandatory, but there are graded worksheets that pop up both during lectures and mostly during discussions which are about 10% of your grade, so you really should go. Also, those worksheets are super helpful to understand what exams are like. As for homework, I'm ngl I did like 3 of them and there were probably around 10-12 not quite sure. The ones I did were helpful but they're all optional and really can just be used as additional studying. Finally, just some interesting policies that Herman has. No phones, laptops, iPads, etc. If using technology is important to you definitely don't take Herman because he is very serious about it and will call you out every single time. Don't sit in the back row because he will tell you to move up. The damn pdf password really got me it's really annoying to have a locked pdf but also thats not really that deep. There is a participation grade for 3% and he is more likely to call on you if you sit in the front (not really that crazy but good to know). He doesn't do Canvas announcements but instead has a newsfeed that won't notify you when he posts and instead you have to remember to check (this really pissed me off but also not that deep, not sure why he does this). You also can't email him or message him because he won't answer, you have to go to office hours to ask any questions and such. Finally, he has very specific style requirements. Most of them were pretty intuitive to me, the only one that sucked was that you aren't allowed to have multiple return statements, that was always so annoying but I got used to it. Overall though, I thought Herman was a very good teacher and I can honestly say I learned so much this semester. Coming from AP Comp Sci A in high school I think it's super important to have a good teacher in 132 for these foundational concepts. I know a lot of people where 132 was more review for them, but for me it was all new and I feel like I learned it very well. I recommend Herman for 132!

If you try to keep an open mind and think in depth about how the course knowledge would apply to some kind of software, you should be able to understand the course content easily. This project is not consistently just coding, and is spaced out well that you should be fine as long as you and your group are dedicated. At times, Golub's grading can hurt you in this project if you aren't careful, so be diligent and read through all of the project requirements in depth. The class project is 46% of your grade, and the tests are 44%. There are four tests (including the final, however the final is not really a final and is worth the same percentage as the other three exams). The tests are where my biggest complaints are. They are entirely open ended, often 5 questions with an average of 2-4 subparts, totaling in around 15 or so paragraphs on average that you have to write. BY HAND! I had less hand cramps during the English section of the SAT, it really sucked. However, I was able to do generally well on the tests because the questions themselves were not hard as long as you studied. There were a couple exams where I ran out of time without being able to complete all of the questions. In summary: nice dude, can be a bit annoying with grading, project is extensive and sometimes hard, tests suck but not that hard. review_text: Pretty polarizing. This review is coming from the perspective of someone who also had Max for 351, so there will be many comparisons. But overall honestly, I think Max has the potential to get somewhat better over time, though this semester was kinda scuffed. Max always said in class that he was more interested in data science than algorithms, but I was somewhat doubtful about whether taking 320 with Max would actually be better. Turns out it is... kind of. This class in general is much easier than CMSC351, so that's one thing for starters. There's a large buffer for your grade in 46% of assignments in the final grade. As the review below mentions, there were many more planned assignments, and they never happened: which wasn't that surprising, given that two (or really one tbh) of the assignments were extremely long. Tests are hit or miss. Coming from 351, there are basically no "Justin" questions (it's almost all Max-y, but there are some questions that are much more direct and less abstract). The first test was highly curved due to poor writing, and honestly, this is something I disliked more than anything besides the abstractness (I honestly found their abstract nature fun at points). Questions are purposely vague, and likely to make you think, but it makes it really easy to misread or gauge a question's intent incorrectly. Now, onto what I think could get better. The 1st assignment was writing... which was fairly useless, and Max realized this for next semester. The second assignment was fairly standard pandas/SQL stuff, but the 3rd assignment is where it got interesting. The 3rd assignment is honestly the best assignment in CS I've gotten ever, which I'm surprised I'm saying. It is VERY messy and very unclear, but that's partially the point, it is honestly the best way to learn stuff, and honestly reminded me of my past work/personal project experience. Probably the best assignment to actually learn, even if it was unforgiving and took forever. I really wish the next 2 assignments had this caliber, but they were quite mundane. I know some people might think I'm crazy for suggesting that he add more assignments like HW3, but I honestly think assignments like those are probably the best way to genuinely learn about data science. Another problem with the homework was that ending concepts didn't really have that much focus in the last assignments, but I also realized that it would have been hard to create interesting homework based on those concepts. Extra credit was quite scuffed this semester. Max initially made it 0.01% of the final grade, and just to put into reference how small this was: 3 notes was supposed to be 0.01%, and he changed it to be 0.05% PER NOTE. That's a 15x change, and frankly, it goes to show how little it was worth (and people thus didn't care much). Again, I do think this will hopefully get better with time. Max's teaching style is sort of like how he was in 351, though he definitely was generally more knowledgeable about the concepts he was teaching (definitely not perfect though). It seems he didn't really care enough to make coherent slides, which led to really vague and hard-to-understand slideshows if you didn't attend the lecture. I think this is probably the most iffy point I have on Max that prevents me from giving him a higher rating because while I do think he will probably change the extra credit system/assignments, I am not sure if he will improve his teaching. Overall though, I'd say Max is a slight upgrade from how he was in 351. As I said, comparatively to 351, this class is nowhere near as hard, though still somewhat poorly managed. Yet, there are some slight shimmers of something great, that makes the class somewhat valuable: maybe not for everyone, but definitely to some.

review_text: I really liked having Marsh for 420 and would highly recommend this experience. This semester is his first semester using a standard-based grading system, so if you completed all of your projects and got 100% on them, got 100% on all of the quizzes, and got a certain amount of “Excellent” for your “exams”, then you would have a guaranteed A. I really liked this style because I knew exactly what I had to complete to get the grade I wanted, and this style forces you to complete your work. There was no curve, and you were not competing with your peers which made the class feel more like a team effort. Like other reviews mentioned, he uses a flipped classroom style so you watch “lecture” videos before class, complete a quiz, and during class, it is like “discussion” where he goes over examples of the data structure. Class kind of felt optional because it was recorded if you really wanted to review it, but he did a good job at keeping track of the notes and posting them if you wanted to reference them later. He is very friendly and knowledgable though, so it was nice to come and support in class. I found this flipped classroom style a little bit difficult for me because it felt like I had to teach myself if I was confused on how to complete the quiz, but this issue was mainly resolved by my next point. There are “soft” deadlines for projects, online quizzes, and online exams (challenge problems) in the class, but you technically have unlimited attempts and until the end of the semester to get 100% on these assignments because you can request for extensions without penalty. If I was confused on how to do a quiz, I could eventually brute force the quiz until I got 100% because the question bank eventually repeats, or I could come to class to watch him do a few more examples and ask questions. The “exams” were not as intimidating as they sound, and I really value Marsh because of the challenge problems. There are 4 problems to complete after each unit, and the questions still force you to understand the data structure (minus all of the theory and math that might be associated with other 420 professors…). I would allocate 1-2 hours to completing the challenge problems per each unit. The final exam was also a set of 4 challenge problems. These exams were little to no stress since if I messed up, then I could get feedback (except for the final) and re-submit. The projects were moderately difficult, but doable if you give yourself enough time and seek out help if you are dying. I would suggest following the soft deadlines that Marsh provides to stay on track because I felt like he gave an appropriate amount of time for each project. I remember he said as long as you dedicate enough time to this class, you can get an A, and I really do agree with this statement.

review_text: I honestly cannot believe I got an A in this course. I remember being so terrified the first week of classes because he started lecturing on the first day and I was already lost and all of my friends had Davis so I was freaking out. The night before the first midterm I literally considered withdrawing (thankfully I didn't). However, I grew to love his teaching style and found his lectures to be interesting. Isaacs is very passionate about organic chemistry and it definitely helped me stay focused during the 75 minute lectures. He can be pretty cold at times but he tends to throw in a few jokes when lecturing which lightens the mood. I've heard he's not the most helpful at office hours but I never went lol. You have to go to lecture for the clicker questions, and honestly if you don't go you will be very lost. I only missed maybe 4 lectures the whole semester and I felt it set me behind when studying. He included about 100 points of clicker questions, which were graded half for accuracy and half for trying. Each midterm was 200 points and the final was 300 points. There are no homeworks so no buffer. Averages were in the 50s-60s and the curve was pretty decent. I had about an 80 in the class, scoring roughly 70s and 80s on the midterms and final, and ended with an A (he guarantees that if you get at least an 80 you will have an A). I was hoping his curve would be a little bigger, sometimes he changes it, but I guess not last semester. His notes are very difficult to read and follow along with after lecture so I tended to mostly use the textbook and took notes on each topic to study. Sometimes the textbook uses different mechanisms than he teaches so make sure to double check things. He included 10+ previous exams WITH answer keys for each midterm which was extremely helpful. Here are my tips for success: -Start studying at LEAST a week before the exam. You can't cram for this class. -Go to discussion and ask questions. I absolutely loved our TA he was amazing and so helpful. -Take notes on the textbook to study. Do all of the practice problems at the bottom of the page. -If you can come up with your own practice problem or explain it to someone else, you probably know the material. -Learn all of the mechanisms for each reaction and make sure you can replicate them. -STUDY OLD EXAMS. This is absolutely key to success. The questions he uses on exams are very similar conceptually to old exams and sometimes even the exact same. -Don't forget about nomenclature. These are freebies on the exams if you study these. Make a quizlet and just go over them once a day if you can. -Go to GSS and office hours. Tbh I never went but I always attended the exam reviews from the GSS leader. I also did his worksheets from the sessions to study. GOOD LUCK!

review_text: By far the worst teacher I have ever had, and hopefully will ever have in my life. I had no idea that teachers could get this bad, and I have had some very bad teachers. To all those interested in taking any of his courses, please read this review in its entirety. There is much to discuss. His lecture style is flying through practice problems and complex concepts as such speed that no one in the class takes notes, because they can't. His lectures are also riddled with errors such that going into lectures with an understanding of the material will leave you with less understanding than what you arrived with. He also rarely posts his slides "to not to compete with the book". Thus, the only way to learn is through the book and scattered online resources, and attending the lectures is a waste of time that you must do because there is a chance of a quiz, which will occur at an unnanounced day every week. If that was all, I would have probably given him 3-4 stars, but alas it gets worse. At the beginning of the semester, he gives out a syllabus that states that every quiz will be based on certain problems from the textbook, that you should do as homework. As you will find out if you take him, that is rarely the case, and the quiz averages will hover near 50%, escalating to a max of 80% for supposedly "easy quizzes". They are not curved. To further the discussion of quizzes, this semester he decided to give out a quiz the day before spring break. He sent an email thereafter containing only the words "attached are notes from class" with a pdf. As students had gotten used to his notes being mostly useless, those who had to miss due to travel/seeing family stuck to reading the book. Attached at the bottom of 26 pages of notes was a 20 point quiz (double the score of all other quizzes) which was to be turned in in class the day after spring break. Those who never saw the quiz were told that he "did all he could do" and they could not take the quiz - they should have known it was attached in an email that had it hidden, with no mention of it in the actual email or any announcement. Thus, university approved absences were nullified. To delve further into the frustration in the difficulty of scoring high in a supposedly grade-boosting portion of the course would not bode well in the interest of time. However the above example should be taken as just that, with the expectation that similar events will occur with relatively high frequency. Since the majority of students struggle with his tests, he issues a makeup for each one. However his makeups are significantly harder than the first ones, and so the average for these is 30 points worse than that of the first one. The tests are uncurved, and if you take the makeup and turn it in it replaces your first score even if it is lower. You may be thinking that this is a very harsh policy, since the tests are already so difficult. You are correct. For our last midterm, he explicitly told us that a certain topic would be on the exam, and it wasn't. In its place was a topic that students didn't study because he stated that "the new material would be represented by a tank mixing problem". Of course, this meant that many students didn't know how to do a quarter of his exam, because there are only 4 questions. Although this is not normal, the tests are hard enough regardless. There are 2 questions each with 2 parts, each 50 points. He also commonly gives students 0 out of 50 for problems that were done slightly wrong, or gives students much less than they should. Sometimes this is fixed with a regrade. Sometimes not. To truly break the camel's back, his exams are only 40 minutes long in a 50 minute lecture period. Now for some miscellaneous points. There are no discussions, which would probably help a lot given the difficulty. Only real homeworks are the matlabs, which are very complex given that the course has 0 coding prerequisites - there is a textbook you must buy to even understand what to do on them. These are supposed to be the real grade boosters - hovering at an average of about 70-80%. Over half of his students currently have failing grades in this course, even accounting for his "curve". Still interested in learning differential equations? I digress to the positives: The final becomes a collective exam score (replacing midterms) if you do better on it than the midterms, but good luck if you think you'll be able to use that. The class is curved such that 680/800 total points is an A, 600/800 is a B, and so on. However as stated above, this is pretty negligable. He seems like a pretty cool person. I almost feel bad leaving this review, and then I remember what his teaching has put me through.

review_text: Kauffman is an amazing CS professor. I would 100% recommend taking him. That being said, here is how his class works: Lectures are 75-minutes, he records everything, but it is still helpful to attend since he is a good lecturer and he takes a lot of questions during lecture. Each time you ask a question, it counts as extra credit. Discussions are pretty much free. We are required to complete at least 10 labs for the course (there are 12 labs in total). The TA will pretty much give the answers to the lab in discussion and you're allowed to collaborate with others on it. On top of that, close to project deadlines, discussions are converted to extra office hours which can be pretty helpful. It is really easy to get a 100% on every homework since it gives you the option to submit each question and the entire form. After every question, it tells you whether or not your answer was right, and you can keep resubmitting until you get all questions right. The projects are very long and difficult. Start early cause office hours (located on the 4th floor of A.V. Williams for some reason) fills up very fast and it can be either very hard or not possible to get help around the project deadline. In terms of difficulty, I found projects 1, 3, and 5 to be the most time consuming. Project 3 was both the most difficult and time consuming since it was the assembly project. The late penalty is very lenient, so there not much of problem with turning them in late. The exams are open note, but they can be quite hard. Rather than focusing on memorizing random things, they try to test big picture concepts and your ability to understand and apply them to sample programs given. There is no multiple choice, only short answer and coding questions. Furthermore, the exams can be a time crunch since almost all questions need a detailed response, so it's very easy to run out of time if you don't manage it on the exam. Despite how hard the projects and exams can be I still recommend taking Kauffman since he is a great teacher, a really nice and helpful person, and you will learn a lot of useful concepts from his class.

review_text: Rainbolt was honestly my favorite professor of the semester -- he was engaging, taught concisely, and was very resourceful in terms of module packets, equation sheets, and giving old practice exams. I felt like I didn't work super hard to earn my grade in the class, but that may be due to general chemistry being easier than orgo. I honestly appreciated his chalk-board + paper packets; it felt more old school and I still wrote down lecture notes on my ipad anyway. Many students complained about his exam problems being different from the module packet, but like...what do you expect? I honestly think he exercised gen chem concepts the way that I wrap them around in my head. If you're good at problem solving, you would excel in his class. It doesn't take long to understand concepts in general chemistry because beyond that, it's just simple math and knowing how to use a calculator. He ensures that his exams aren't memorization based because everything is on his formula sheet, and barely takes points off for calculation errors; he just wants to make sure that your path to getting to the answer is correct. I also thought he was a pretty funny guy in class and his jokes were good; he likely toned it down from previous semesters because I did hear some strange things from previous students. I would say give Rainbolt some grace because he has a strong knack for teaching.

review_text: READ THIS REVIEW. She is not as bad as all these reviews are making her seem. In fact, I think she is a pretty good professor. PROS: Spends a good chunk of class doing practice to help students understand the concepts (which a lot of reviews don't mention because they dont go to lecture). Spends time after class talking to students and helping them understand exam concepts. Records all lectures. Cares about your success, sends out study plan assignments which are free points (although they are pretty useless). The quizzes are not that hard and four lowest of them get dropped. NON CUMALITIVE final which is HUGE for such a content heavy course. Also has a very organized canvas. Very well put together slides. The discussion is pretty straightforward, just groupwork and a lot of exam review sessions which are very helpful. MIDS: Exams are pretty hard but that can be a good thing. If you are someone who relies only on memorization then you will not do good on these exams. You need to be able to understand and APPLY what you have learned, which can be helpful for people who dont want to only memorize. The FRQs are fair and often similar to the practice set and exam review problems. The multiple choice are usually harder in my experience. If you like to use your brain and not just mindlessly memorize things then this exam structure is for you. Her curve is okay, most exam averages were around 60% and the cutoffs for final grades were 87 for an A 77 for a B and 65 for a C. Quizzes, homework's, and lab assignments will help boost your grade . CONS: Oftentimes it felt easier to read off of her slides than go to lectures. She is a decent lecturer but nothing special. Her grading policies were kind of obscure during the class, we always knew what exam scores corresponded to what letter grade but it was pretty unclear on what the actual "curve" would be. She isn't the most warm and welcoming professor, but isn't rude or disrespectful either. Overall, take Prof Mutz if you want a genetics class that doesn't have a cumulative final and midterms that are more than just memorization. Her lectures feel optional but the practice in them can be very helpful. Make sure to stay on top of lab assignments and pay attention to the plethora of exam review material she gives.
evidence_snippet: The quizzes are not that hard and four lowest of them get dropped.
label_rationale: Clear evidence supports exam heavy, homework heavy, disorganized course.
